meta.title: Irish A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Irish → English (see the Irish, recall the meaning) and English → Irish (see an English meaning, recall the Irish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Irish has a CEFR examination, Teastas Eorpach na Gaeilge (TEG), but it publishes syllabuses of topics and grammar rather than a graded word list, so this deck is not TEG's vocabulary or any examination's, and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 281 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, question words, prepositions and particles every sentence is built out of — and the other 219 are the commonest remaining words, counted by the WHOLE word (every form of a noun or a verb together) over two corpora: a treebank of written Irish and a collection of everyday sentences, a word joining only if the everyday sentences use it. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Spellings are the Official Standard's (An Caighdeán Oifigiúil), and verbs are given, as Irish dictionaries give them, by their command form (déan, 'do!'). Under each headword is its pronunciation in IPA, labelled with the dialect it belongs to — Irish has no single standard pronunciation, and Connacht, Munster and Ulster differ. The 253 nouns show their gender, which decides how the article changes the noun (an bhean, 'the woman'; an fear, 'the man'), with their genitive and plural, and behind the All forms fold their forms with the article and their lenited and eclipsed forms; the 69 verbs show their past, verbal noun and future, and a regular verb its tenses by person; a preposition shows its forms with each pronoun (agam, agat, aige …). Real example sentences come with 455 of the 500 words, three apiece for 346 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Irish Dependency Treebank (Universal Dependencies UD_Irish-IDT, CC BY-SA 3.0) and Tatoeba. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
